::: {.callout-note title="Title justification (per project criteria)"}
"Amplification" is, by definition, an **interaction**: the effect of rainfall on coastal nutrients
is *larger where anthropogenic stressors are present*. The evidence meets the project's criteria for
the strongest title. (1) The rainfall × cesspool and rainfall × agriculture interactions are both
positive and significant after controlling for terrestrial connectivity (log SiO₂) and spatial
structure (@tbl-coefs; @fig-interactions). (2) Adding these interactions improves spatially blocked
out-of-sample prediction (Model C leave-one-ahupuaʻa-out R² = 0.376 vs 0.316 for delivery-only). (3)
The **rainfall × cesspool** amplification holds when any one of the three smaller islands is
excluded (β = 0.17–0.21, all p < 0.02; @tbl-loio), though it is anchored in Oʻahu — 53% of samples
and the dominant cesspool gradient — and weakens when Oʻahu is removed (β = −0.42, p = 0.28). The
rainfall × agriculture interaction is strong overall (β = 0.66, p = 0.002) but concentrated on Maui
(β = 0.24, p = 0.57 without Maui) and is reported as island-specific. The additive main effects were
never the test of amplification; the conditional interaction is, and it is robust. The nutrient-form
contrast (Si vs N vs P vs NH₄) remains a supporting result rather than the headline.
:::

## Abstract

Extreme rainfall episodically couples land and sea, yet the mismatch between storm timescales and
routine monthly monitoring means these pulses are rarely observed at scale. In March 2026 a Kona
Low delivered island-mean rainfall of 68–124 mm day⁻¹ across Hawaiʻi. A distributed community
science network sampled coastal water chemistry at 746 locations across four islands (Oʻahu, Maui,
Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi) 12–26 days after peak rainfall, spanning 132 ahupuaʻa (traditional watersheds) —
a window during which conventional monitoring recorded no samples. Relative to contemporaneous
high-salinity marine-background water, storm-influenced samples were enriched ~4.8× in dissolved
silicate (SiO₂), ~2.0× in NO₃+NO₂, ~1.8× in PO₄, and ~1.6× in NH₄. Against a decade of
fixed-station monitoring (Hui o Ka Wai Ola), March 2026 was the wettest month on record and drove
network nutrient anomalies to the 98th–100th percentile of the decade, with individual stations
reaching up to 41× their historical baseline. Spatially explicit generalized additive mixed models
showed that the four nutrient forms record different stages of the land-to-sea pathway: SiO₂
delivery was governed by physical connectivity and hydrologic forcing, while NH₄ was the least
spatially coherent and least predictable at watershed scale. Critically, human land use *amplified*
the coastal nitrogen response to rainfall: significant rainfall × cesspool and rainfall ×
agriculture interactions show that the same storm delivered more NO₃+NO₂ where wastewater and
agricultural pressures were denser, and adding these interactions improved spatially blocked
out-of-sample prediction. The rainfall × cesspool amplification held when any of the three smaller
islands was excluded, though it was anchored in Oʻahu, which carried most samples and the strongest
cesspool gradient. The results reframe
the standard "large storm = large pulse" expectation as "large storm × landscape = coastal
exposure," and show that extreme events reveal — and amplify — the coastal signature of chronic
anthropogenic nutrient sources.

## Introduction

Tropical island coastlines are tightly coupled to their watersheds. Steep terrain, permeable
volcanic substrate, and short transit distances mean that terrestrial water — both surface runoff
and meteoric groundwater — can reach the coast rapidly, carrying dissolved nutrients that shape
nearshore biogeochemistry. In Hawaiʻi, prior work has shown inverse salinity relationships for
nitrate+nitrite, phosphate, and silica along the Kona coast, and demonstrated that land use and
groundwater flow paths strongly determine nutrient fluxes to coastal waters. Yet the episodic
events that likely dominate annual land-to-sea transport are poorly resolved: storm pulses operate
on timescales of hours to days, while routine monitoring is typically monthly, so the largest
fluxes are systematically undersampled.

Extreme rainfall offers a natural experiment. A single storm simultaneously perturbs hundreds of
adjacent watersheds that differ in topography, soils, and human modification, allowing the
controls on coastal nutrient delivery to be estimated across a gradient rather than one catchment
at a time. We use the March 2026 Kona Low, sampled by a distributed community science network, to
ask four questions:

- **Q1.** How large and spatially heterogeneous was the coastal nutrient pulse?
- **Q2.** Was the 2026 event unusual relative to normal temporal variability?
- **Q3.** What watershed properties control *where* nutrients reach the ocean?
- **Q4.** Does human land use amplify coastal nutrient enrichment beyond hydrologic delivery alone?

Our conceptual framework treats dissolved silicate — enriched in Hawaiian terrestrial water
through basalt weathering — as a tracer of *how strongly land and ocean are connected*, and treats
nitrogen and phosphorus, relative to that connection, as indicators of *how nutrient-rich the
delivered water is*. We deliberately analyze the four nutrient species separately rather than as a
single water-quality index, because they record different segments of the pathway.

## Methods

### Study region and sampling design

Coastal water samples were collected by a community science network across four Hawaiian Islands
between 28 March and 8 April 2026, 12–26 days after peak storm rainfall. Sampling was organized by
ahupuaʻa, the traditional Hawaiian watershed unit, which we use as the primary spatial unit for
aggregating landscape predictors (~650 ahupuaʻa exist across the four islands; 132 were sampled).
Each sample records latitude/longitude, collection time, island, and the four dissolved nutrient
responses: NO₃+NO₂, PO₄, NH₄ (reported as the analytical variable `NH3`), and SiO₂. Salinity was
measured concurrently and used only to define storm-influenced versus marine-background water and
for event validation, never as a mechanistic response.

### Storm context and rainfall metrics

Event rainfall was characterized from CHIRPS (~5 km daily) for 10–31 March 2026. For each sampled
watershed we extracted cumulative storm rainfall (the primary event-exposure variable), plus 3-day
maximum, 7-day core-storm total, peak-day rainfall, and days since peak. For long-term context we
used monthly island-mean CHIRPS (2016–2026). Storm discharge came from USGS gauges (nearest gauge
within 15 km); antecedent soil wetness from NASA POWER GWETROOT.

### Landscape covariates

Predictors were grouped *a priori* into four conceptual sets to avoid post hoc storytelling:
(A) hydrologic forcing (cumulative storm rainfall, storm discharge, antecedent soil wetness);
(B) watershed transport/connectivity (distance to stream mouth, mean slope, soil saturated
hydraulic conductivity, Ksat); (C) anthropogenic sources (cesspool exposure index, cesspool
density and buffer counts, % agriculture, % impervious, population density, distance to
NPDES-permitted discharge); and (D) coastal dilution/retention (wave fetch, significant wave
height). Sources and transformations are in @tbl-sources. Cesspool coverage combined the Hawaiʻi
HCPT layer (Oʻahu/Maui) with the DOH OSDS 2010 inventory for Molokaʻi; the cross-source vintage
difference is a documented comparability caveat, and models were re-run with and without Molokaʻi.

**Cesspool exposure index.** The primary cesspool metric is a distance-decay exposure index computed
per sample from the combined cesspool point layer. For each sample $i$, exposure is the sum of
exponentially distance-weighted contributions from every cesspool $j$ within a 2,500 m cutoff:

$$\text{exposure}_i = \sum_{j:\,d_{ij} \le 2500\text{ m}} \exp\!\left(-\,d_{ij}\,/\,b\right),$$

where $d_{ij}$ is the sample-to-cesspool distance (m) and $b = 500$ m is the bandwidth (the cutoff of
2,500 m is five bandwidths, at which the weight is ≈0.007 and negligible beyond). A nearby cesspool
therefore contributes more than a distant one, and multiple nearby cesspools accumulate, so the index
increases with both proximity and abundance. Distances were computed in projected UTM zone 4N
(EPSG:32604). This single index supersedes the separately collinear buffer-count and
distance-to-nearest metrics (Spearman |r| ≈ 0.79), and yields a well-defined value of 0 on Lānaʻi
(no cesspools within the cutoff) rather than a missing value, so cesspool exposure enters the primary
four-island model directly. The index was `log1p`-transformed and then standardized (z-scored) for
modeling (reported as `log(cesspool exposure)` in @tbl-coefs).

### Data analysis

*The analysis is fully scripted and reproducible in `kona_low_nutrient_analysis.qmd`, with a single
global random seed, `here::here()` paths, and all model objects saved as `.rds`.*

**Sample flow and quality control.** We began from the raw chemistry table and built an explicit
sample-flow audit rather than complete-case filtering. One record with fully missing metadata was
dropped, leaving 746 georeferenced samples. Because ahupuaʻa names recur across islands, every
watershed-level join used the composite key {ahupuaʻa, island}, and island names were normalized
to a single apostrophe encoding before joining. A stable `site_id` was assigned from unique
coordinate pairs (sites nearly equal samples: e.g., 379 sites among 406 Oʻahu samples), and
`sample_id` was retained. Reported zeros were treated as below-detection-limit and substituted with
DL/2, with original flags retained for sensitivity analysis. **Response-specific sample sizes were
used throughout** — a sample missing NH₄ still entered the NO₃+NO₂ model — so *n* varies by model
and is reported for each (SiO₂ *n* = 657, NO₃+NO₂ *n* = 611, PO₄ *n* = 583, NH₄ *n* = 366).

**Transformation and distributional checks.** All four nutrients are right-skewed with
below-detection values and were modeled on the log scale after inspecting zeros, detection-limit
values, and extremes. Fold enrichment (storm ÷ marine background; salinity threshold 34 PSU) was
estimated with 4,999 bootstrap replicates and percentile 95% CIs.

**Long-term extremity (Q2).** Using Hui o Ka Wai Ola fixed stations (2016–2026), we computed
station-normalized fold changes (concentration ÷ station historical median; ≥6 pre-2026 obs per
station) and paired monthly medians with monthly CHIRPS rainfall. We fit the routine
log(fold change) ~ log(rainfall) relationship on **pre-2026 months only** (*n* = 116) and asked
whether the observed March 2026 anomaly fell outside the 95% prediction interval, and where March
2026 ranked in the pre-2026 distribution.

**Spatial structure (Q3).** For each nutrient we computed global Moran's I (k-nearest-neighbor
weights, k = 10) on log1p concentrations, overall and per island, plus empirical variograms for
the two well-sampled islands (@fig-variograms). Kriging was used for visualization only
(@fig-spatial), masked to a narrow coastal buffer with observed points overlaid, never as evidence
of concentration where no samples exist.

**Nutrient-specific models (Q3–Q4).** We fit spatially explicit generalized additive mixed models
(`mgcv`) with a common structure per nutrient: log(response) as a function of the standardized
group-A–D predictors, island terms, an ahupuaʻa random effect to handle pseudoreplication
(multiple samples per watershed share landscape covariates), and a two-dimensional spatial smooth
of coordinates to absorb residual spatial autocorrelation. Predictors were standardized so
coefficients are directly comparable across models (@tbl-coefs). We first modeled log(SiO₂) on
delivery predictors only (the terrestrial-connectivity model), then modeled log(NO₃+NO₂),
log(PO₄), and log(NH₄) including log(SiO₂) as a delivery covariate plus the anthropogenic
predictors, so anthropogenic effects are estimated *net of* how much terrestrial water was
delivered. A priori interactions (stream distance × slope; rainfall × cesspool; rainfall ×
agriculture; rainfall × Ksat; cesspool × Ksat) were tested; only conceptually justified terms were
retained. Collinearity was assessed with Pearson/Spearman correlations and VIF; no predictor was
dropped on an arbitrary VIF rule.

**Human-amplification test (Q4).** For NO₃+NO₂ we compared three nested models under identical
spatial cross-validation: **Model A** (delivery + connectivity + coastal), **Model B** (A +
additive anthropogenic terms), and **Model C** (B + rainfall × anthropogenic interactions). We
additionally partitioned deviance across driver blocks (M0 spatial/island → M1 hydrology → M2
connectivity → M3 anthropogenic → M4 coastal) for all nutrients (@fig-varpart). To probe whether the
amplification slope differed among islands, we also refit the primary NO₃+NO₂ interaction model with
an island-level random slope on the rainfall × cesspool product term (`s(island_f, rc, bs = "re")` in
`mgcv`), and — because a random-effect variance over only four islands is weakly identified — we
complemented it with leave-one-island-out refits of the fixed interaction (@tbl-loio).

**Cross-validation.** Because neighboring samples are not independent, we used blocked spatial
cross-validation: leave-one-ahupuaʻa-out (LOAO) for realistic predictive skill and
leave-one-island-out (LOIO) for cross-island generalizability (@fig-loio). We report R², RMSE, MAE,
and calibration slope for all four nutrients. A random forest was fit per nutrient (continuous
response, spatial CV, permutation importance) purely for the applied hotspot-prediction question —
not for causal inference.

**Sensitivity analyses.** Primary NO₃+NO₂ results were re-estimated under alternative
transformations, with/without extreme observations, with/without island terms, with/without the
spatial smooth, with/without log(SiO₂), under site-date aggregation, under alternative cesspool and
land-use metrics, and with/without Molokaʻi (@tbl-sensitivity). Model diagnostics (residual vs
fitted, QQ, residual maps, residual Moran's I, observed vs predicted) were produced for every final
model; a model was not accepted as final if residual spatial autocorrelation remained strong.

## Results

### Q1 — A large, spatially heterogeneous, nutrient-specific pulse

The network captured 746 samples across 4 islands and 132 ahupuaʻa in a 12-day window
(@tbl-sampling; @fig-sampling). Storm-influenced water (≤34 PSU, *n* = 426) was enriched relative
to contemporaneous marine-background water (>34 PSU, *n* = 320), but the magnitude differed
markedly by nutrient form (@fig-distributions):

| Nutrient | Storm median | Background median | Fold enrichment |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SiO₂ | 19.1 | 3.97 | **4.8×** |
| NO₃+NO₂ | 1.64 | 0.83 | 2.0× |
| PO₄ | 0.25 | 0.14 | 1.8× |
| NH₄ | 0.33 | 0.20 | 1.6× |

: Storm-influenced vs marine-background medians (µmol L⁻¹) and median fold enrichment. {#tbl-fold}

The storm signal was strongest for SiO₂ and oxidized nitrogen and weakest for reduced nitrogen —
the first indication that the nutrient forms behave differently. Island medians (@tbl-sampling)
show Maui and Molokaʻi with the highest NO₃+NO₂ and SiO₂, and NH₄ elevated on Molokaʻi.

### Q2 — March 2026 sat at the extreme upper tail of the decadal record

March 2026 was the single wettest month in the 2016–2026 Maui CHIRPS record (rank 1 of 117 months;
373 mm — about 1.35× the next-wettest month, December 2021, and more than 2× the next-wettest
March). Network-monthly-median fold changes ranked at the 98th–100th percentile of all pre-2026
months (NO₃+NO₂ 98th, PO₄ 100th, SiO₂ 98th). Individual stations reached far higher values — up to
41× the station baseline for NO₃+NO₂ at Mala Ramp, West Maui (@fig-context; @fig-station-fc).

The routine relationship between monthly rainfall and network nutrient anomalies is weak (log–log
R² = 0.05 for NO₃+NO₂, 0.08 for PO₄; SiO₂ slope not significant, p = 0.87 — consistent with SiO₂
tracking terrestrial-water *connectivity*, which varies spatially, rather than rainfall amount at a
fixed point). Tested against the 95% prediction interval of that routine relationship, only the PO₄
network median clearly exceeded expectation; NO₃+NO₂ (observed 1.7×, interval upper bound 2.04×)
sat at the 98th percentile but *within* the wide prediction interval. We therefore describe March
2026 as producing coastal nutrient conditions at the extreme upper tail of the decadal record —
most cleanly exceeding routine expectation for PO₄ and reaching station-level NO₃+NO₂ extremes —
rather than as a formal threshold exceedance for all nutrients.

### Q3 — Spatial structure and the controls on delivery

All four nutrients were significantly spatially clustered on the log1p scale, with a clear
ordering: SiO₂ (global Moran's I = 0.49) > NO₃+NO₂ (0.35) > PO₄ (0.32) > NH₄ (0.23; all p ≪ 0.001).
NH₄ was significantly clustered on every island but at the shortest spatial scale — it is the most
*localized*, not unclustered (@fig-spatial; @fig-variograms).

The **SiO₂ delivery model** (deviance explained 49.9%) was dominated by physical and hydrologic
predictors (@tbl-coefs): cumulative storm rainfall (standardized β = +0.44), proximity to stream
mouths (log distance β = −0.30), and coastal exposure (wave height β = −0.35, fetch β = −0.23) all
had CIs excluding zero, while watershed slope and Ksat did not. This supports interpreting SiO₂ as
an indicator of terrestrial-water delivery whose strength is set by how strongly a stretch of coast
is hydrologically connected to land and how quickly delivered water is flushed.

### Q4 — Nutrient forms record different stages of the pathway

Standardized coefficients from the four models (@tbl-coefs; @fig-effects) tell contrasting stories:

- **NO₃+NO₂** (dev. expl. 59.6%) was governed first by **terrestrial delivery** (log SiO₂
  β = +0.77) and hydrologic forcing (storm rainfall β = +0.61), then by land use: % agriculture
  (β = +0.46), cesspool exposure (β = +0.14), and proximity to NPDES discharge (β = −0.16) all had
  CIs excluding zero. Both a priori interactions were significant: **rainfall × cesspool**
  (β = +0.20) and **rainfall × agriculture** (β = +0.66) — human-source enrichment is larger where
  hydrologic forcing was stronger.
- **PO₄** (dev. expl. 54.2%) was likewise led by delivery (log SiO₂ β = +0.40) and rainfall
  (β = +0.23), with a weaker cesspool signal (β = +0.07) and a negative impervious/wave-height
  association. No rainfall × source interaction was significant. PO₄ enrichment is therefore mostly
  a delivery/transport phenomenon with a modest source component; we do not treat PO₄ as a specific
  wastewater tracer.
- **NH₄** (dev. expl. 37.1%) was the least explained and least spatially coherent. Only log SiO₂
  (β = +0.26) had a CI excluding zero; no anthropogenic predictor was significant. This is
  consistent with reduced inorganic N being controlled at finer spatial and biogeochemical scales
  (localized inputs, rapid cycling, redox/sediment processes) than oxidized N — offered as
  hypotheses, not conclusions.

**Human land use amplifies the coastal nitrogen response to rainfall.** The central result is a
conditional (interaction) effect — the operational definition of amplification: the slope of coastal
NO₃+NO₂ on storm rainfall increases with anthropogenic source density (@fig-interactions). Both a
priori interactions were significant in the primary model: **rainfall × cesspool** (β = 0.20,
p = 0.002) and **rainfall × agriculture** (β = 0.66, p = 0.002). Three lines of evidence establish
that this is genuine amplification rather than an artifact:

1. *It improves out-of-sample prediction.* In spatially blocked cross-validation of nested NO₃+NO₂
   models, Model A (delivery only) had LOAO R² = 0.316; adding only **additive** anthropogenic terms
   (Model B) did not help (R² = 0.300); adding the **rainfall × source interactions** (Model C)
   raised skill to R² = 0.376 (ΔR² ≈ +0.06). The predictive gain comes specifically from the
   conditional term.
2. *The cesspool amplification is robust across most island exclusions but Oʻahu-anchored.*
   Refitting the interaction model while dropping each island in turn (@tbl-loio), the
   rainfall × cesspool interaction held when Lānaʻi (β = 0.21, p = 0.003), Maui (β = 0.20,
   p = 0.012), or Molokaʻi (β = 0.17, p = 0.017) was excluded, but weakened to non-significance and
   changed sign when Oʻahu — the majority of samples and the dominant cesspool gradient — was
   removed (β = −0.42, p = 0.28). The rainfall × agriculture interaction, by contrast, is strong
   overall but concentrated on Maui (β = 0.24, p = 0.57 with Maui removed) and should be interpreted
   as island-specific. A complementary model with an island-level random slope on the
   rainfall × cesspool term left the population-level interaction unchanged (β = 0.20, p = 0.002) and
   estimated a negligible between-island slope variance (SD ≈ 0.005 on the standardized scale;
   ΔAIC ≈ 0), but with only four islands that variance component is effectively unidentifiable (95%
   CI spanning dozens of orders of magnitude), so the leave-one-island-out refits above — not the
   random slope — carry the informative evidence on between-island heterogeneity.
3. *Sources add nutrients even before conditioning on rainfall.* The additive cesspool effect is
   also significant within-sample (β ≈ 0.14, p ≈ 0.03) and stable across most sensitivity
   specifications (@tbl-sensitivity); its small additive-only contribution to variance partitioning
   (@fig-varpart) simply reflects that the human signature is expressed most strongly *during* the
   storm — i.e., as amplification — rather than as a rainfall-independent offset.

For context, terrestrial delivery remains the dominant control on *where* nutrients arrive: after
spatial/island structure and hydrology, the connectivity/delivery block (log SiO₂) added ~+17.5 pp
of deviance for NO₃+NO₂ and ~+17.6 pp for PO₄ (@fig-varpart). Amplification acts on top of that
delivery — it governs *how nutrient-rich* the delivered water is where human pressures are dense.

**Predictive skill and generalizability.** LOAO spatial CV R² was moderate for NO₃+NO₂ (0.38) and
PO₄ (0.37), lower for NH₄ (0.16) and SiO₂ (0.10). Leave-one-island-out CV was substantially worse
(SiO₂ overall R² negative; @fig-loio), indicating that relationships learned on three islands
transfer poorly to a held-out fourth — a real limitation for extrapolation across islands.

**Sensitivity.** The primary NO₃+NO₂ cesspool coefficient was consistent in sign and roughly in
magnitude across transformations, island handling, aggregation, and land-use metric swaps
(@tbl-sensitivity). It weakened under a sqrt transform (p = 0.60) and without the spatial smooth
(p = 0.078), and — as expected — strengthened when log(SiO₂) was omitted (β = 0.215, p = 0.005),
confirming that delivery and source are partially collinear and must be modeled jointly.

## Discussion

**Extreme events reveal land–sea connections routine monitoring misses.** During the storm window,
conventional monitoring recorded no samples, whereas the community science network captured 746
observations across four islands. Dense, opportunistic sampling directly addresses the mismatch
between storm timescales and monthly monitoring, and shows that the largest coastal nutrient
signals occur precisely when standard programs are blind.

**The same storm does not produce the same coastal exposure everywhere.** Enrichment varied over
orders of magnitude among sites and differed systematically by nutrient form. Physical
connectivity and hydrologic forcing — not rainfall amount alone — determined where terrestrial
water reached the coast. This shifts the interpretation from "large storm = large pulse" to "large
storm × landscape = coastal exposure."

**Extreme events amplify chronic anthropogenic pressures.** The clearest human signal was an
amplification — a conditional interaction rather than a rainfall-independent offset. The slope of
coastal NO₃+NO₂ on storm rainfall was steeper where cesspools and agriculture were denser
(@fig-interactions), so the same storm delivered more coastal nitrogen to watersheds carrying more
human nutrient load. This is the mechanism the strongest title names: long-term land and
infrastructure decisions set *what is available for transport*, and extreme hydrologic forcing is
what mobilizes it. The rainfall × cesspool amplification is robust to removing any of the three
smaller islands but is anchored in Oʻahu, which holds most of the data and the strongest cesspool
gradient (the interaction weakens when Oʻahu is removed; @tbl-loio); the rainfall × agriculture
amplification, though strong in the pooled data, is concentrated on Maui and is reported as
island-specific. We frame these as
amplification of source signatures under extreme forcing, not proof that any single source caused
elevated nitrate: cesspools, agriculture, and permitted discharge are spatially correlated and
cannot be fully disentangled with these data.

**Different nutrients record different stages of the land-to-sea pathway.** SiO₂ reflects
terrestrial-water connectivity; NO₃+NO₂ reflects connectivity plus nitrogen sources and their
conditional mobilization; PO₄ reflects connectivity with a smaller source/geochemical component;
and NH₄ is controlled at finer spatial and biogeochemical scales, making it the least predictable
from watershed variables. Reading the four species jointly, rather than as a single water-quality
index, is what makes the mechanism visible.

**Limitations.** Predictive skill is moderate and cross-island transfer is weak (LOIO), so
island-specific processes remain important and extrapolation beyond sampled watersheds is not
warranted. Sampling occurred 12–26 days after peak rainfall, so the measured pulse is a post-peak
snapshot, not the flux maximum. Molokaʻi cesspool data derive from a different source and vintage;
within-island relative comparisons are more defensible than cross-island magnitude comparisons.
Discharge coverage is sparse (63% missing), so stream-mouth distance, not gauged discharge, carried
the connectivity signal.

## What the analyses actually support

**Three strongest supported conclusions**

1. Human land use amplifies the coastal nitrogen response to extreme rainfall. Significant
   rainfall × cesspool and rainfall × agriculture interactions (both p = 0.002) show that the same
   storm delivered more NO₃+NO₂ where anthropogenic sources were denser; the interactions improve
   spatially blocked out-of-sample prediction (Model C LOAO R² = 0.38 vs 0.32), and the
   rainfall × cesspool effect survives excluding any of the three smaller islands (though it is
   anchored in Oʻahu; @tbl-loio).
2. A single extreme rainfall event produced widespread but spatially heterogeneous coastal nutrient
   enrichment across four islands, with magnitude differing strongly by nutrient form (SiO₂ ~4.8× >
   NO₃+NO₂ ~2.0× > PO₄ ~1.8× > NH₄ ~1.6× over marine background), and terrestrial-water connectivity
   (log SiO₂, stream proximity, rainfall, coastal flushing) explains *where* storm-derived nutrients
   reach the coast.
3. The four nutrient forms carry contrasting landscape signatures: SiO₂ and NO₃+NO₂ are spatially
   coherent at watershed-to-coast scales, whereas NH₄ is the most localized and least predictable.

**Suggestive but uncertain**

- The rainfall × agriculture amplification is strong overall but concentrated on Maui; it should be
  reported as island-specific until corroborated elsewhere.
- March 2026 pushed coastal nutrient anomalies to the 98th–100th percentile of the decade and drove
  station-level NO₃+NO₂ to ~41× baseline, but formal exceedance of the routine rainfall–nutrient
  prediction interval was clear only for PO₄, and the historical network is limited to Maui.

**Not supported (as stated in the aspirational story)**

- A large *additive*, rainfall-independent human offset. The anthropogenic signature is expressed
  chiefly as amplification (conditional on rainfall); additive-only terms add little to variance
  partitioning or out-of-sample skill.
- Strong cross-island predictive generalization of the full models: leave-one-island-out CV of
  absolute concentrations was poor, so magnitudes should not be extrapolated to unsampled islands.
- PO₄ as a specific wastewater tracer, or specific NH₄ mechanisms — these remain
  descriptive/hypothetical.

**Which title is justified.** The strongest title —
*"Extreme rainfall reveals human amplification of land-to-sea nutrient transport across tropical
coastlines"* — is justified: the amplification is a cross-validated, spatially structured
interaction whose cesspool term survives excluding any of the three smaller islands (though it is
Oʻahu-anchored; @tbl-loio). The nutrient-form contrast is a well-supported supporting result.

The community science network sampled 746 coastal locations across 132 ahupuaʻa on 28 March–8 April, 12–26 days after peak rainfall — a window in which conventional monitoring recorded no samples. Scale bars at lower-left of each map panel; basemap Esri World Imagery.](output/main_figures/Fig1_sampling_map.png){#fig-sampling}

![Coastal nutrient concentrations by salinity group: storm-influenced (≤34 PSU; orange) and marine background (>34 PSU; blue), for NO₃+NO₂, PO₄, NH₄, and SiO₂ (µmol L⁻¹). Each point is one sample (jittered); violins show the empirical distribution and the bold crossbar the median. Annotations give the median fold enrichment, median(storm)/median(background), with 95% bootstrap CI (4,999 replicates). Below-detection samples are excluded from the plotted points (NO₃+NO₂ n = 44; PO₄ n = 77; NH₄ n = 185; SiO₂ n = 27); medians lie well above detection limits so fold estimates are unaffected. Enrichment is strongest for SiO₂ (~4.8×) and NO₃+NO₂ (~2.0×) and weakest for NH₄ (~1.6×).](output/main_figures/fig2_nutrient_distributions.png){#fig-distributions}

![Long-term context for March 2026. (A) Monthly Maui island-mean rainfall (CHIRPS, 2016–2026); March 2026 (373 mm; orange triangle) was the wettest month in the record (rank 1 of 117). (B–D) Monthly station-median fold change (observed / station pre-2026 median) versus monthly rainfall for NO₃+NO₂, PO₄, and SiO₂ on log–log axes, with the pre-2026 fit (n = 116 months) and its 95% prediction interval; the orange triangle marks March 2026. The routine rainfall–nutrient relationship is weak (R² = 0.05–0.08) and non-significant for SiO₂ (slope p = 0.87). At the network-median level, only PO₄ exceeded the prediction interval; NO₃+NO₂ and SiO₂ were at the 98th percentile but within the interval, while individual stations reached far higher fold changes.](output/main_figures/fig3_rainfall_nutrient_context.png){#fig-context}

![Spatial distribution of coastal nutrient concentrations following the March 2026 Kona Low. Rows: NO₃+NO₂, PO₄, SiO₂, NH₄ (µmol L⁻¹); columns: Oʻahu, Maui, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi. Oʻahu, Maui, and Molokaʻi use ordinary kriging on log1p concentrations (spherical variogram; minimum range = island diagonal/5; 3 km coastal band; 250 m grid; sample-coverage masking prevents extrapolation into unsurveyed coast). Lānaʻi shows raw sample locations only (n = 20). Filled circles are individual samples on the same color scale as the surface; the scale is shared across islands within each nutrient row. Kriging is for visualization only. NO₃+NO₂ and SiO₂ form the most spatially coherent hotspots, whereas NH₄ is the most localized (global Moran's I 0.23 vs 0.49 for SiO₂). Scale bars at lower-left of each panel.](output/main_figures/fig4_spatial_nutrients.png){#fig-spatial}

![Standardized fixed effects on NO₃+NO₂ from the four-island model, ordered by effect size within each mechanistic group. Filled circles mark effects whose 95% CI excludes zero; open circles mark non-significant effects. Predictors are grouped by mechanism: terrestrial delivery (log SiO₂), hydrologic forcing (storm rainfall), watershed transport (topography, soils), anthropogenic sources (cesspool exposure, agricultural and impervious cover, distance to permitted discharge), coastal dilution (wave exposure), and the two significant rainfall × source interaction terms. Terrestrial delivery and hydrologic forcing are the largest effects; agriculture and cesspool exposure add positive anthropogenic signal, and the interaction terms show that rainfall conditionally amplifies NO₃+NO₂ where anthropogenic sources are denser. Island/ahupuaʻa random effects and the spatial smooth are not shown. Parallel standardized effects for PO₄, NH₄, and the SiO₂ delivery model appear in the Supplement.](output/main_figures/fig5_nox_primary.png){#fig-effects}

![Conditional amplification of coastal NO₃+NO₂ by anthropogenic land use during extreme rainfall. Marginal predictions from the primary NO₃+NO₂ model show how the storm-rainfall relationship with predicted NO₃+NO₂ steepens with (A) cesspool exposure index — the primary and most robust amplification result — and (B) % agricultural land cover. Lines are population-level predictions (island, ahupuaʻa, and spatial random effects excluded) holding other predictors at their means; the three lines per panel correspond to the 10th (low; blue dashed), 50th (median; grey solid), and 90th (high; red dashed) percentiles of the moderator. Positive interaction slopes indicate stronger rainfall-driven enrichment where sources are denser. **Panel A (primary result):** the rainfall × cesspool interaction is significant (β = 0.20, p = 0.002), improves spatially blocked out-of-sample prediction (Model C leave-one-ahupuaʻa-out R² = 0.38 vs 0.32 for delivery-only), and holds when any one of the three smaller islands is excluded, though it is anchored in Oʻahu (@tbl-loio). **Panel B:** the rainfall × agriculture interaction is strong in the pooled data (β = 0.66, p = 0.002) but concentrated on Maui (β = 0.24, p = 0.57 without Maui) and is interpreted as island-specific. The y-axis is capped at 78 µmol L⁻¹ (99th percentile of observed NO₃+NO₂); in Panel B the high-agriculture line exceeds this cap at extreme rainfall, a sparse region of predictor space where the divergence direction is meaningful but the absolute magnitude is not reliable.](output/main_figures/fig6_interactions.png){#fig-interactions}

## Tables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sampling
#| tbl-cap: "Sampling summary by island: number of samples, sites, and ahupuaʻa; date range; and median [IQR] concentration (µmol L⁻¹) for each nutrient."
read_tbl("table1_sampling_summary.csv") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Island", "n samples", "n sites", "n ahupuaʻa", "Date range",
                      "NO₃+NO₂", "PO₄", "NH₄", "SiO₂"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Predictor variables: process represented, spatial scale, source, transformation, and missingness."
read_tbl("table2_data_sources.csv") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Variable", "Process", "Scale", "Source", "Transformation", "Missing"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "Standardized fixed-effect estimates [95% CI] for the four nutrient models (SiO₂ delivery model; NO₃+NO₂, PO₄, and NH₄ interaction models). * indicates a 95% CI excluding zero. Predictors are grouped by mechanism."
read_tbl("table3_model_coefficients.csv") |> kable()
```

## Supplementary tables

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loio
#| tbl-cap: "Leave-one-island-out robustness of the two NO₃+NO₂ amplification interactions. The interaction model was refit dropping each island in turn (identical formula and cesspool metric). β is the standardized interaction coefficient; * marks p < 0.05. The rainfall × cesspool amplification holds when any one of the three smaller islands is removed but weakens and changes sign when Oʻahu (53% of samples, dominant cesspool gradient) is removed; the rainfall × agriculture amplification is significant only when Maui is retained."
read_tbl("tableS_loio_interactions.csv") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Specification", "n", "Rain × cesspool β", "p", "", 
                      "Rain × agriculture β", "p", ""))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the primary NO₃+NO₂ result across analytical specifications: deviance explained, standardized cesspool coefficient, its p-value, and whether the sign/magnitude is consistent with the primary model."
read_tbl("tableS_sensitivity_overview.csv") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Specification", "Dev. expl. (%)", "Cesspool β", "Cesspool p", "Consistent"))
```

West Maui stations dominate the extreme high end for NO₃+NO₂ (up to 41× at Mala Ramp); PO₄, SiO₂, and NH₄ panels show different spatial structure.](output/supplement/suppfig_station_fold_changes_mar2026.png){#fig-station-fc}

![Empirical variograms for log1p-transformed nutrient concentrations (Oʻahu and Maui; UTM zone 4N). Point size scales with pairs per bin. SiO₂ shows the clearest distance-decay structure on both islands (highest global Moran's I, 0.49); NH₄ shows the weakest spatial structure (0.23).](output/supplement/figS2_variograms.png){#fig-variograms}

![Variance partitioning among mechanistic driver-group blocks (% deviance explained from the nested M0→M4 GAM sequence) for the four nutrients. Connectivity/delivery dominates the between-watershed signal for NO₃+NO₂ and PO₄; the additive anthropogenic block adds little (<2 pp). Shares are descriptive increments sensitive to entry order, not independent causal contributions.](output/supplement/figS6_variance_partition.png){#fig-varpart}

![Leave-one-island-out cross-validation: observed versus predicted concentrations for the four nutrients, holding out each island in turn. Cross-island transfer is weak (SiO₂ overall R² negative), indicating that relationships learned on three islands do not reliably predict the fourth.](output/supplement/figS7_loio_obs_pred.png){#fig-loio}

## Data and code availability

All data sources are catalogued in @tbl-sources. The complete analysis, figures, tables, and saved
model objects are in `kona_low_nutrient_analysis.qmd`; outputs are under `output/`. Session
information is recorded via `sessioninfo::session_info()`.
